entry.title: [推荐] Rethinking (De)growth: the politics of compost
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Jessica Croteau

Moving beyond economic analyses of degrowth, growth and consumption are reframed through decomposition as a vital process through which life, value, and politics are continually re-composed. Against dominant imaginaries that cast decay as waste or ruination, this article turns to composting and carrion ecologies to articulate decomposition as a generative undoing and a mode of transformation that binds waste to worth. Drawing on multispecies examples from vultures in India to the Baltimore Compost Collective, the article situates decomposition as both material process and political metaphor to enact a revaluation of growth, decay, and consumption that unsettles capitalist logics of extraction and accumulation. entry.title: [推荐] The subject of intelligence: AI as existential risk and the government of the human and the future
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Caio Simoneti

This article analyses discourses on artificial intelligence (AI) in the field of existential risk studies. AI appears as a key theme in existential risk circles, not only as a source of risk, but also as a resource for risk prevention and as the enabler of a glorious future for humanity. However, what is it about AI that brings together utopian and dystopian imaginaries? Why is a discourse on AI so tied to questions regarding the human, and what forms of humanity does it produce? What forms of governing does it enable? This article argues that the concept of ‘intelligence’ is fundamental regarding both how AI is construed as an existential risk, as well as how humanity is conceptualised as that which needs to be protected. entry.title: [推荐] From universalism to situated universality: reconfiguring Kantian pacifism
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (5.0)

Naomi Ellis

In Toward Perpetual Peace , Kant argues that war’s violence enables humanity to envision perpetual peace as both reason’s moral end and history’s presumptive telos, thereby motivating action to renounce war. This article critiques the universalist assumption underlying this argument and argues instead for a pacifism grounded in what I call ‘situated universality’. I do so through a comparative political theoretical approach. After reconstructing Kant’s account of peace, I turn to post-World War II Japan, where a Kantian defense of its pacifist constitution initially flourished, but was later challenged by a nationalistic counter-discourse. entry.title: [推荐] Difference‐Making Under Metaphysical Indeterminacy
entry.content:
Philosophy & Public Affairs · Vol. 54 No. 4 262-273 · 推荐 (4.0)

Jessica Li

Many of the most pressing moral problems we face involve collective harms generated by large numbers of individually insignificant actions. Unlike triggering cases—where a threshold exists such that a single act could be decisive—non‐triggering cases lack any such sharp cutoff. In these cases, no individual act appears to make a difference to whether harm occurs, and it may be metaphysically indeterminate whether a given aggregate is harmful or whether a marginal contribution plays any causal role at all. I argue that standard approaches to moral responsibility, which rely on difference‐making or expected outcomes, struggle to provide action‐guiding reasons in these contexts. entry.title: [推荐] Is religion a problem for intersectional theory? Muslim women, feminism, and varieties of patriarchy
entry.content:
Contemporary Political Theory · Vol. 25 No. 1 · 推荐 (3.0)

Karolin I. M. Tuncel、Tobias Müller

Intersectional theory has been criticised for neglecting religion and for being unable to account for religion’s social complexities. This contribution interrogates this critique by disaggregating different relationships of Muslim women to secular and religious varieties of patriarchy. We argue that what demarcates the challenges of intersectional analysis are the political contestations not around religion, but around women’s pro-patriarchal agency. We do so by discussing intersectional theory’s analytical usefulness and limitations in conceptualising the experiences of Muslim women. Political Theory · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.0)

Samuel Piccolo

This article is about an internal contradiction within the ascendant philosophy of new materialism, namely that its ethical opposition to harm clashes with its ontology. In the first part, I summarize new materialists’ attention to material entanglements and rejection of hierarchies in nature. In the second section, I argue that diagnosing and addressing harm to ecosystems and individuals (almost) always depend upon a hierarchy of beings within that ecosystem and a set of pre-determined potentials/preferences of how individual entities should be, two principles that new materialists explicitly reject. Toby Rollo

In this article I ask whether the main traditions of Western political thought, republicanism, conservatism, liberalism, and socialism, can supply an account of human flourishing capable of sustaining a broad antifascist movement. Each tradition defines full humanity as an achievement reserved for the mature adult and treats the child as a being in preparation, excluded from the sites of genuine political agency and human actualization. I refer to this shared framework as the metaphysics of maturity. entry.title: [推荐] The Closure Problem in Discourse Ethics: Ecological Truth and the Limits of the Tripartite Model
entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 推荐 (3.0)

Michael Hemmingsen

Discourse ethics rests on the assumption that validity claims fall into a closed triad: facts about the objective world, norms about the intersubjective world, and self‐expressions disclosing the subjective world. This paper challenges that assumption. I argue that the tripartite framework is not exhaustive, and that treating it as such generates a previously unrecognized form of exclusion: not at the level of access, power, or expression, but at the level of intelligibility itself. To make this case, I introduce “ecological truth” as a candidate for a distinct kind of validity claim. Drawing on examples from place‐based discursive practices, I suggest that such claims are plausibly neither factual, normative, nor self‐expressive, but exhibit a different structure of validity grounded in long‐term ecological relationships and practices of attunement. Current theoretical literature discusses leadership executive in terms of symbolic representation but outside of public administration philosophers have ignored process representation. entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (15.2)

Efe Basturk

This article develops a critical account of human rights through an encounter between Jacques Derrida and Jacques Rancière. Rather than treating their approaches as complementary components of a single theory, I argue that their disagreement reveals two irreducible dimensions of the politics of rights: the situated enactment of equality and the temporal non‐closure of every such enactment. Rancière shows how rights become political when those excluded from an existing distribution invoke their egalitarian inscriptions to stage a dissensus and enact themselves as political subjects. entry.content:
Constellations · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (9.7)

Monica Adami

This article revisits Agamben's state of exception. Homo Sacer and State of Exception frame camps as spaces where law is suspended and life reduced to “bare life.” This decisionist paradigm underestimates the institutional and economic complexity of refugee management. This article proposes the concept of sovereignty by omission: Exclusion produced not by a decisive suspension of law but by legal ambiguity, bureaucratic deferral, and systemic inaction. Engaging Schmitt, Benjamin, Foucault, and Butler, the article situates omission within debates on sovereignty and rights and develops the argument through the case of Gaza. entry.title: [必读] Beyond the consumer: Stiegler’s economy of contribution and the politics of care
entry.content:
Theory, Culture & Society · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (7.0)

Conceição Soares

This article explores the economy of contribution as an alternative to consumerist capitalism, rooted in free software practices and digital commons. Drawing on Bernard Stiegler’s critical theory, particularly his reflections on proletarianization, care, and technological pharmacology, this model reconfigures traditional producer-consumer roles toward collaborative value creation and long-term social, ecological, and cognitive investment. The argument is grounded in the Plaine Commune project in France, which experiments with contributive income, collaborative urban planning, and co-constructed therapeutic practices, demonstrating how contributory models can foster knowledge, autonomy, and collective responsibility. Theory, Culture & Society · 预印(online-first) · 必读 (7.0)

Zhongkai Qian、Ngai Pun

This article closely examines Giorgio Agamben’s philosophical and methodological framework, especially the notions of oscillation and threshold, and their limits. On the one hand, Agamben insightfully exposes the paradoxes of modern biopolitical structures and, in turn, seeks to dissolve the binary between zoē and bios by addressing form-of-life as a liberating unity. This article argues that, on the other hand, Agamben’s oscillatory approach contributes to a dialectic of potentiality and political passivity. By dissecting the threshold as a liminal interface – neither advancing nor retreating – Agamben’s political ontology remains ambiguous about messianic time.
